topics.title: E.2 A Team Wants to Delete Receipts After One Hour
topics.summary: Scenario. Receipt storage is growing. An operator proposes deleting every row older than one hour while leaving the API’s replay promise unchanged.

blocks.text: E.2 A Team Wants to Delete Receipts After One Hour
rich: E.2 A Team Wants to Delete Receipts After One Hour

rich: Receipt storage is growing. An operator proposes deleting every row older than one hour while leaving the API’s replay promise unchanged.
blocks.headingContext: E.2 A Team Wants to Delete Receipts After One Hour

blocks.text: Reasoning. Receipt retention determines the temporal boundary of duplicate recognition. After deletion, a delayed request can be treated as new. Storage reclamation is therefore a contract change, not only a maintenance task.
rich: Receipt retention determines the temporal boundary of duplicate recognition. After deletion, a delayed request can be treated as new. Storage reclamation is therefore a contract change, not only a maintenance task.
blocks.headingContext: E.2 A Team Wants to Delete Receipts After One Hour

blocks.text: A defensible policy could define a key validity period and reject old requests outside it, archive searchable receipts, or maintain another durable summary with a justified collision and retention model. The policy must account for queued retries, disconnected clients, backups, and replay tools.
rich: A defensible policy could define a key validity period and reject old requests outside it, archive searchable receipts, or maintain another durable summary with a justified collision and retention model. The policy must account for queued retries, disconnected clients, backups, and replay tools.
blocks.headingContext: E.2 A Team Wants to Delete Receipts After One Hour

blocks.text: Verification. Create a completed operation, advance a controlled retention clock, prune under the proposed rule, and replay the old key. The expected result must match the documented policy. A test that merely verifies fewer rows after cleanup says nothing about replay safety.

topics.title: E.3 A Gateway Should Use Several Workers

blocks.text: E.3 A Gateway Should Use Several Workers

blocks.text: Scenario. The gateway is changed to select a random port from three workers, each with its own SQLite file. All ordinary requests succeed, so the team claims horizontal scaling is complete.

blocks.headingContext: E.3 A Gateway Should Use Several Workers

blocks.text: Reasoning. A retry can reach a worker that lacks the original receipt. Local uniqueness in each file does not create a global authority. The design needs shared transactional state, partitioned ownership with migration rules, or a replicated service with the required consistency.

blocks.headingContext: E.3 A Gateway Should Use Several Workers

blocks.text: A fixed key-to-worker mapping helps only while membership and state placement remain coordinated. Adding or removing a node can move a key away from its receipt. The migration must carry the idempotency state and handle stale routing views.

blocks.headingContext: E.3 A Gateway Should Use Several Workers

blocks.text: Verification. Commit at worker A, lose the reply, route the retry to B, and inspect effects. This deliberately failing history exposes the missing authority. A corrected design must preserve the invariant under that history and during membership changes, not merely under a stable hash function.

topics.title: E.4 A Database Callback Must Leave the Reactor Thread
topics.summary: Scenario. Database contention causes long handler pauses. A developer moves each SQLite call to a detached thread and captures the peer object by reference.

blocks.text: E.4 A Database Callback Must Leave the Reactor Thread
rich: E.4 A Database Callback Must Leave the Reactor Thread

blocks.text: Scenario. Database contention causes long handler pauses. A developer moves each SQLite call to a detached thread and captures the peer object by reference.
rich: Database contention causes long handler pauses. A developer moves each SQLite call to a detached thread and captures the peer object by reference.
blocks.headingContext: E.4 A Database Callback Must Leave the Reactor Thread

blocks.text: Reasoning. The change removes one synchronous wait while creating lifetime and resource problems. The peer can expire or the server can stop before the detached thread completes. Unlimited threads can also replace bounded peer state with unbounded execution resources.
rich: The change removes one synchronous wait while creating lifetime and resource problems. The peer can expire or the server can stop before the detached thread completes. Unlimited threads can also replace bounded peer state with unbounded execution resources.
blocks.headingContext: E.4 A Database Callback Must Leave the Reactor Thread

blocks.text: Use a bounded executor with explicit operation state. The task owns the request data it needs. Completion returns to the designated state owner and checks whether the peer generation is still eligible. Shutdown stops admission, cancels or drains work under policy, joins execution, and only then releases shared state.
rich: Use a bounded executor with explicit operation state. The task owns the request data it needs. Completion returns to the designated state owner and checks whether the peer generation is still eligible. Shutdown stops admission, cancels or drains work under policy, joins execution, and only then releases shared state.
blocks.headingContext: E.4 A Database Callback Must Leave the Reactor Thread

blocks.text: Verification. Delay a database completion until after peer expiry and after server drain begins. Verify no stale reference is accessed, no response is written to a reused connection identity, and accepted durable work remains recoverable even when the original peer is gone.

topics.title: E.6 A Broker Consumer Wants More Parallelism
topics.summary: Scenario. A consumer processes offsets 100 and 101 concurrently. It records checkpoint 102 when 101 finishes first.

blocks.text: E.6 A Broker Consumer Wants More Parallelism
rich: E.6 A Broker Consumer Wants More Parallelism

blocks.text: Scenario. A consumer processes offsets 100 and 101 concurrently. It records checkpoint 102 when 101 finishes first.
rich: A consumer processes offsets 100 and 101 concurrently. It records checkpoint 102 when 101 finishes first.
blocks.headingContext: E.6 A Broker Consumer Wants More Parallelism

blocks.text: Reasoning. If the checkpoint represents the next unprocessed offset, it has skipped unfinished 100. The consumer needs a contiguous-completion frontier or a different supported transaction protocol. Processing order and checkpoint order cannot be inferred from delivery order once concurrency is introduced.
rich: If the checkpoint represents the next unprocessed offset, it has skipped unfinished 100. The consumer needs a contiguous-completion frontier or a different supported transaction protocol. Processing order and checkpoint order cannot be inferred from delivery order once concurrency is introduced.
blocks.headingContext: E.6 A Broker Consumer Wants More Parallelism

blocks.text: If effects are external to the broker transaction, retain an application inbox or another effect-side deduplication mechanism. A replay after crash must not apply the completed operation again merely because its checkpoint was not retained.

blocks.headingContext: E.6 A Broker Consumer Wants More Parallelism

blocks.text: Verification. Complete 101, crash before 100, restart, and verify that 100 is processed while 101’s retained effect is not duplicated. A test that processes all offsets in order never exercises the gap.
rich: Complete 101, crash before 100, restart, and verify that 100 is processed while 101’s retained effect is not duplicated. A test that processes all offsets in order never exercises the gap.

reading.title: E.12 Write a Filled Architecture Decision Record
paragraphs: Decision. Use one worker receipt authority and a durable gateway pending table for the teaching service.

Context. The application must preserve a stable key’s meaning across lost replies and process restarts. The domain is intentionally small, the deployment is local-only, and the instructional priority is an inspectable recovery argument.

Alternatives considered. Pure in-memory retries would lose intent on restart. Independent random workers would not share receipts. A production replicated broker/database stack would add capabilities but obscure the small example’s ownership and deployment requirements.

Consequences. The service has a clear local transaction boundary and real process tests, but no high availability, global deduplication across independent stores, public authentication, or bounded historical retention. Pending capacity is bounded; total durable history is not.

Evidence. Domain, storage, framing, policy, and process tests exercise the stated invariants. The final report identifies actual compiler configurations and limitations. The source listings are assembled from the same files used by those tests.

Revisit triggers. A requirement for multiple state owners, public access, long-term retention limits, strict latency isolation, or terminal-failure workflows requires a new design and verification plan. It is not a reason to silently reinterpret the existing guarantees.

This record is short because it names the decision and its consequences directly. A useful architecture document does not need to predict every future framework. It needs to let the next engineer understand why the current boundary exists and what evidence must change before replacing it.

33.title: Appendix E — Architecture Review Exercises and Worked Reasoning

sections.title: Read and apply
sections.purpose: These exercises ask for decisions and evidence rather than memorized terminology. Each scenario changes one assumption of the teaching service. The worked reasoning identifies the invariant

sections.title: E.1 A Client Wants to Retry with a New Key
sections.purpose: Scenario. The client submitted annual7 with input 25 and timed out. A user-interface developer proposes retrying with annual8 so the second attempt will not conflict with anything left behin

sections.title: E.2 A Team Wants to Delete Receipts After One Hour
sections.purpose: Scenario. Receipt storage is growing. An operator proposes deleting every row older than one hour while leaving the API’s replay promise unchanged.

sections.title: E.3 A Gateway Should Use Several Workers
sections.purpose: Scenario. The gateway is changed to select a random port from three workers, each with its own SQLite file. All ordinary requests succeed, so the team claims horizontal scaling is complete.

sections.title: E.4 A Database Callback Must Leave the Reactor Thread
sections.purpose: Scenario. Database contention causes long handler pauses. A developer moves each SQLite call to a detached thread and captures the peer object by reference.

sections.title: E.5 A Cache Should Serve Every Status Query
sections.purpose: Scenario. A cache stores MISSING for a key, then the gateway accepts that key. A client immediately checks status and receives cached missing.

sections.title: E.6 A Broker Consumer Wants More Parallelism
sections.purpose: Scenario. A consumer processes offsets 100 and 101 concurrently. It records checkpoint 102 when 101 finishes first.

sections.title: E.7 A New Schema Changes Units
sections.purpose: Scenario. A field named timeout previously meant milliseconds and now means seconds. The field type and tag remain unchanged, so the team calls the change wire-compatible.

sections.title: E.8 A Dashboard Reports Perfect Success During Overload
sections.purpose: Scenario. The metric denominator includes only jobs that reached the worker. The gateway rejects most new work as busy, but worker success remains 100 percent.

sections.title: E.9 A Backup Restores Only the Gateway
sections.purpose: Scenario. The gateway is restored from yesterday while the worker retains today’s receipts. Some completed jobs no longer appear in gateway status.

sections.title: E.10 A Circuit Breaker Should Be Shared Across Threads
sections.purpose: Scenario. Several threads call the single-owner breaker model directly because its methods are short and its fields are integers.
